summary:
Western Australia's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects one attribute relevant to trans people: "gender history", defined in the statute and in state government guidance as living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex. Guidance published by the state government and updated on 12 February 2026 states that direct and indirect discrimination on this ground are unlawful, and that treating a person as their former sex is a form of direct discrimination. The attribute is not framed as gender identity, so the state's protection is worded more narrowly than the gender-identity grounds used in several other Australian jurisdictions.

Eligibility to complain is tied to legal recognition. Gender history is established through a recognition certificate or a recorded change of sex or gender under the births, deaths and marriages framework, which means a trans person who has not amended Western Australian identity documents may sit outside the complaint mechanism even where the treatment described is discriminatory. The Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet records that the 2024 recognition reforms amend section 4(1) of the Act to delete the "gender reassigned person" definition and insert one keyed to certificates or registration, that the amendment does not operate retrospectively, and that complaints will have to satisfy the new registration requirements once it commences.

The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 was assented to on 26 September 2024 and took effect on 30 May 2025. It repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, which the Premier and Attorney-General described at introduction on 16 April 2024 as the last body of its kind in the country. Medical and surgical reassignment are no longer prerequisites; a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, replaces the board process. Male, female, indeterminate/intersex and non-binary descriptors are available, a change may be made once a year, the fee is A$195 and non-refundable, and processing takes up to four weeks. Applicants under 18 need parental consent or the permission of the Family Court of Western Australia. The Act carries a statutory review clause after three years.

The removal of surgical prerequisites has a longer history in the state. Sterilisation was required before 2012, until the High Court held on 6 October 2011 in AB v Western Australia that two trans men who had undergone bilateral mastectomies and androgen therapy were entitled to male recognition certificates without hysterectomy, oophorectomy or genital reconstructive surgery. The requirement that an applicant be unmarried was repealed by legislation that passed both chambers in early 2019 and commenced on 19 March 2019.

Complaints go to the state Commissioner of Equal Opportunity, with a 12-month lodgement window, acknowledgment of receipt within one week and a free conciliation conference as the next step. A complainant may instead use the federal route to the Australian Human Rights Commission under national sex discrimination law within 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters, but only one route may be chosen. TransFolk of WA and the Freedom Centre, the latter for people under 26, provide trans-specific support in the state.

Prison policy reported in November 2020 allows transgender prisoners to be housed according to their gender identity for health and safety reasons, provided their criminal record carries no sexual offences. Placement turns on that record check rather than operating as an unconditional entitlement.

No law in Western Australia prohibits conversion practices. The government said a bill would be introduced only after the March 2025 state election; as of September 2026 Western Australia and Tasmania were the only Australian jurisdictions without an explicit criminal prohibition, leaving Western Australia the only mainland state where the practices remain lawful. A Public Order Bill that would criminally ban harassment on grounds of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics passed the lower house but had not passed the upper house. Announced reforms to the Equal Opportunity Act would add gender identity and sex characteristics as protected attributes and repeal the exemption allowing religious schools to discriminate; neither change had been enacted.

In October 2021 the Western Australia Supreme Court removed a transgender child from parental custody entirely over continuing abuse, the first order of its kind in the country, following the April 2021 death of a 15-year-old trans teenager in Perth that prompted calls to reform the birth-certificate law.
tangentialFactors:
The recognition reform was announced on 16 April 2024 as one part of a wider package: a replacement Equal Opportunity Act and a ban on conversion practices were both signalled for 2025. Only the recognition Act has passed, so the state's anti-discrimination statute still uses the older "gender history" formulation and still contains the religious-schools exemption.

The 2024 Act's three-year statutory review clause means the annual-change limit, the A$195 non-refundable fee and the clinical-statement requirement are all revisitable, but no review body or terms of reference are set out in the material available.

Western Australia's protected attribute is narrower than the gender-identity grounds used in several other Australian states, and the announced Equal Opportunity Act rewrite is the mechanism by which that gap would close. Until it passes, a trans visitor relying on state law in Western Australia is working with a definition drafted around transition and certification rather than around identity as such.

The Public Order Bill's progress is a live variable: lower-house passage has been recorded, upper-house passage has not, and the criminal harassment protection it would create on gender-identity grounds therefore does not yet exist.
localsOnly:
Residents pursuing a state complaint file with the Commissioner of Equal Opportunity within 12 months of the conduct, receive acknowledgment within a week, and are offered a free conciliation conference. The federal alternative at the Australian Human Rights Commission runs to 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters, and the two routes are mutually exclusive, so the choice is made once.

Changing a birth certificate now runs through the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages rather than a board: a supporting statement from a doctor, nurse or psychologist, A$195 non-refundable, up to four weeks, one change per year, and male, female, indeterminate/intersex or non-binary descriptors. Under-18 applicants need parental consent or Family Court of Western Australia permission.

Because complaint eligibility under the Equal Opportunity Act is keyed to a recognition certificate or a registered change, residents who have not completed that process may find their discrimination claim limited, and the 2024 amendment to section 4(1) will require complaints to meet the new registration requirements once it commences.

Trans-specific support is available from TransFolk of WA and, for people under 26, the Freedom Centre. Prisoners may be housed according to gender identity where their record carries no sexual offences. Conversion practices remain lawful in the state, and the announced ban had not been introduced at the time of the source material.
outOfScopeNotes:
Commencement of the 2024 recognition Act is described inconsistently across the sources: the Equal Opportunity Commission fact sheet treats it as passed with commencement still to be proclaimed, while other material records it taking effect on 30 May 2025. The proclamation instrument itself was not reviewed, and the interim handling of gender-history complaints before commencement is not sourced.

The High Court decision in AB v Western Australia is dated 6 October 2011 in one source and 2012 in another. The 2011 date matches the reported judgment; the 2012 reference is unresolved.

Whether the replacement Equal Opportunity Act and the conversion practices bill were introduced after the March 2025 state election is not established by the sources, and the upper-house fate of the Public Order Bill remains open.

The practical operation of the prison housing policy, including how the sexual-offence record check is applied and whether placement decisions are reviewable, is not documented in the material available.
